brand_003:n1.prompt:
You are helping me generate color palette directions for my brand based on a set of brand adjectives (the descriptive words that define our brand personality, e.g., 'bold, trustworthy, modern' or 'warm, playful, approachable'). 

First, ask me for: (1) my brand adjectives (3-5 words), (2) my company/domain name, and (3) any existing brand constraints (e.g., a color we must include, an industry norm to avoid, accessibility requirements like WCAG contrast compliance).

Once I provide these, do the following:
1. Translate each adjective into color psychology associations (e.g., 'trustworthy' often maps to blues, 'playful' to bright/warm hues).
2. Propose 3 distinct palette directions, each with a clear name/theme (e.g., 'Confident Blue', 'Warm Optimism', 'Modern Minimal'). For each direction, specify: a primary color, one or two secondary/accent colors, and a neutral (background/text) color, each with hex codes.
3. For each palette, briefly explain how it reflects the given adjectives and note its likely emotional tone.
4. Flag any accessibility concerns (e.g., low contrast between text and background) for each palette.
5. Present the three directions in a clear side-by-side summary (table or bulleted comparison) so I can easily evaluate trade-offs.

Done looks like: three well-differentiated, named palette directions, each with hex codes for primary/secondary/neutral colors, a rationale tying back to my adjectives, and accessibility notes — ready for me to review and pick one (or request adjustments) in the next step.

Report back with the full comparison and your recommendation for which direction best fits the stated adjectives, along with reasoning. Do not finalize or lock in a palette — this is a proposal step only.

brand_003:n2.prompt:
You are helping me choose a direction for our brand color palette. This is a subjective creative decision, so your job is to prepare well-researched options for me to review and decide on — not to make the final choice yourself.

First, ask me for any details you need if I haven't already given them: our company/domain name, a short description of what we do, our target audience, our industry, any competitor brands to differentiate from or align with, and any existing brand assets (logo, colors already in use) I should account for.

Then do the following:
1. Research color psychology and palette conventions relevant to our industry and audience.
2. Use a tool like Coolors (or similar palette generator) or your own design knowledge to generate 4-6 distinct palette directions (e.g., "bold and energetic," "minimal and trustworthy," "warm and organic," etc.), each with a short name and 1-2 sentence rationale tying it to our brand and audience.
3. For each direction, list the actual hex codes for a primary color, a secondary color, an accent color, and a neutral/background color.
4. Briefly note any competitor or industry conventions each direction aligns with or deliberately breaks from.
5. Compile all of this into a single clear document or message, organized so I can quickly compare directions side by side.

Done looks like: I have a concise, well-organized set of 4-6 palette direction options with hex codes, rationale, and industry context, ready for me to review.

Report back with the full list of palette directions and their details, then stop for human sign-off — do not select a final direction, apply any colors to brand assets, or make the choice on my behalf. Wait for me to tell you which direction I want to move forward with.

brand_003:n3.prompt:
You are helping me finalize the brand color palette for my organization by checking WCAG contrast and accessibility compliance before it's locked in.

First, ask me for anything you need that isn't already provided:
- My domain or brand name
- The current candidate color palette (hex codes for primary, secondary, accent, background, and text colors)
- Any existing style guide, logo, or brand asset references
- Whether I have specific use cases to check (e.g., button text on brand background, links on white, dark-mode variants)

Once you have the palette, do the following:
1. Compute contrast ratios for all realistic foreground/background pairings likely to appear in the product or marketing site (e.g., body text on background, button label on button fill, link color on background, white text on dark brand color).
2. Evaluate each pairing against WCAG 2.1 standards: AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text (18pt+/14pt bold+) and UI components; note where AAA (7:1) is also met.
3. Flag every pairing that fails AA, and for each failing pair propose one or two adjusted hex values (slightly darker/lighter shades of the same brand color) that would pass while staying visually close to the original intent.
4. Check the palette for color-blind safety (e.g., avoid relying on red/green alone to convey meaning) and note any concerns.
5. Produce a clear table: color pair, hex codes, contrast ratio, pass/fail for AA and AAA, and recommended fix if failing.

Done looks like: a complete contrast audit table covering all key pairings, with pass/fail status and concrete hex-code remediation suggestions for any failures, plus a short summary of overall accessibility risk.

Report back with the full table, the summary, and a final list of the recommended (possibly adjusted) palette hex codes ready for my review. Do not change official brand assets or publish anything — just prepare this analysis, since finalizing the palette remains a human step.

brand_003:n4.prompt:
You are helping me set our finalized brand color palette as design tokens (variables) inside {{vendor}}, our design tool. 

Before starting, ask me for: (1) the final list of brand colors with names and hex values (e.g. Primary, Secondary, Accent, Neutral shades, Success/Error/Warning if defined), (2) the {{vendor}} workspace/team or project where these tokens should live, and (3) whether we need multiple modes/themes (e.g. Light and Dark) or just one default mode.

Once you have this, using your configured credentials and {{vendor}}'s API or plugin/token-management interface:
1. Create or open the relevant design file/library in {{vendor}}.
2. Create a color variable/token collection for our brand palette if one doesn't already exist.
3. Add each brand color as a named token with the correct hex value, matching the names I gave you.
4. If multiple modes were requested, set up those modes and assign correct values per mode.
5. Verify the tokens are saved and visible in the tool's variables/tokens panel, and that names and values exactly match what I provided.
6. If the API/plugin surface requires publishing or enabling library sharing for the tokens to be usable across files, complete that action as it is a routine configuration step, not a sign-off decision.

When done, report back: the name of the token collection/library, the full list of tokens created with their names, hex values, and mode assignments (if any), and a link or path to where they live in {{vendor}}. If any color name was ambiguous or you had to make a judgment call on naming/structure, flag it clearly in your report so I can review. Do not invent colors or modes I have not provided — ask me if anything is missing.
